records.title: Enhanced Ethanol Ablation for Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
records.current_registry_description: Some cancer patients have a poor prognosis, despite intensive multimodal therapy (e.g., surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy). In other cases, these treatments are likely to improve outcome but are inaccessible (e.g., financial, scheduling and/or geographical limitations). Thus, there is an immense need for treatments that offer effective tumor control and palliation, and that ideally can be given at low-cost in the primary care setting. We have recently demonstrated proof-of-concept for a low-cost effective option, called enhanced ethanol ablation. Ethanol ablation (intratumoral injectionof pure ethanol) was originally used for human liver cancer, achieving survival rates similar to surgical resection for small tumors. However, conventional ethanol ablation is ineffective for superficial, large, and/or poorly encapsulated lesions, and requires large injection volumes. Enhanced ethanol ablation involves controlled injection of an ethyl cellulose- ethanol mixture directly into the tumor. When mixed with ethyl cellulose, a water-insoluble ethanol-based gel is formed. We have shown this caused complete regression in 7 of 7 chemically-induced tumors in the hamster oral cavity while dramatically reducing the required injection volume. Now, we will perform a pilot study to evaluate safety and efficacy in feline oral squamous cell carcinomas, which serves as a model for other large, superficial and invasive tumors. Cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (mandibular and maxillary) will be enrolled. They will have basic staging tests performed, and then undergo anesthesia for a intratumoral injection of ethyl cellulose-ethanol. The tumor will be imaged using CT, before and after injection. Cats will be hospitalized overnight for observation, after this first injection. They will then return for periodic recheck exams to evaluate for toxicity and changes in tumor size. Depending on response to the first injection, cats may be eligible for up to 2 booster injections. Cats will be dismissed from the study at the time of local disease progression, or after 6 months of follow-up.

records.title: Ethos Precision Medicine Umbrella Study for Hemangiosarcoma (Ethos-PUSH)
records.current_registry_description: Canine splenic hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer with limited treatment options available. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Roughly 40% of dogs have benign splenic disease causing the internal bleeding and will be cured with surgery alone. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. For dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma, the combination of surgery and chemotherapy has been estimated to provide median survival times of 4-9 months with only a small percentage of dogs surviving to 2 years. Ethos-PUSH embarks on a journey to improve the outcome of canine hemangiosarcoma by furthering our understanding of this disease. Dogs confirmed to have hemangiosarcoma will be randomized to receive 1 of 4 treatments. These treatment groups include standard therapies and novel therapies that have been selected as potential targets against previously defined genomic alterations in hemangiosarcoma. Treatment arms will be compared to determine a best protocol, which will serve as the benchmark for future treatment studies. Furthermore, tumor and blood samples will be collected and serve as platforms for nationwide collaborations to improve the molecular understanding of this disease and match molecular biomarkers with treatment response to specific therapeutics. This comprehensive approach is designed to bring about curative outcomes for dogs suffering from this aggressive cancer. records.title: Minimally Invasive Metastasectomy in Canines (MIMIC) Trial
records.current_registry_description: Following surgical removal of the primary tumor and treatment with chemotherapy, the spread of cancer to the lungs (metastasis) is the most common cause of mortality in dogs with many tumors. A distinctive feature of lung metastases in human patients is the surprising benefit that can result from surgical removal of the lung metastases. The use of surgery to manage lung metastases in dogs has been described but is not commonly used due to the presumed post-surgical complications associated with conventional open chest surgery (thoracotomy). Innovations in minimally invasive surgery have created a new opportunity to include surgical removal of lung metastases with a reduced potential of complications when compared to the conventional thoracotomy techniques. Conventional thoracotomy techniques can be replaced by thoracoscopy, a surgical technique using miniature incisions in the chest to allow for removal of lung metastases with the assistance of a magnified video camera. This approach has the potential to significantly minimize the pain, potential complications, and recovery time in patients compared to what is observed with conventional thoracotomy techniques. Using minimally invasive surgery, specifically video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), we predict patients will be recovered from the procedure within 2 days and will be able to begin to return to normal life. The goal of our study is to assess the feasibility and tolerability of VATS for lung metastasis and eventually deliver this care as an outpatient procedure. records.title: COTC033: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers: Validation in Canine Patients
records.current_registry_description: This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of a Vaccine Peptide Library (VPL) when given to dogs with cancer. This clinical trial conducted in pet dogs with cancer is designed to test whether the immune responses generated through routine vaccination against common viruses can be re-directed toward cancer cells. The approach appears to work in mouse models of cancer, and we are interested in evaluating it in pet dogs that have naturally occurring cancers that are very similar to humans. If successful, this research would help develop safe, effective, and low-cost ways of treating cancer that would benefit a wide variety of patients, especially those that live in communities with minimal access to cutting-edge cancer care (such as developing and low-resource countries). Studies in dogs with cancer will complement currently open human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent. As part of this study, your dog will be randomized to receive one of two vaccine protocols: either combination treatment with Shingrix/Garadasil vaccines or a rabies vaccine. Your dog will come to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital for the primer phase, which includes 1-3 weekly injections of the vaccines. Two weeks later, they will return to start weekly visits for injection of the VPL directly into the tumor for 8 weeks. Dogs will be treated with diphenhydramine (Benadryl) prior to the injection and then will be monitored for 4-6 hours post-injection. One final visit will be required one week after the last injection (total length of study 12-14 weeks). Physical exam and blood collections for study purposes will be performed at each visit. A complete blood count will be performed every week during the treatment phase; blood and urine for serum chemistry profile and urinalysis will also be collected on Weeks 1, 5, and 9. Chest x-rays +/- abdominal ultrasound will be checked prior to the primer vaccine and at Week 9. Lymph node aspirates for study purposes will be obtained at Weeks 1, 5, and 9 of the treatment phase. Biopsies of your dogs tumor will also be collected prior to the first dose of the drug (pre-treatment), on Week 5, Week 5 at 24hrs, and Week 9 depending on how your dog has responded to therapy. Each of these biopsy sessions will occur under anesthesia, either local (sedation with anesthetic) or general.

records.title: Efficacy and safety of a novel anti-cancer therapeutic for the treatment of metastatic mammary carcinoma in cats
records.current_registry_description: Purpose of Study:Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade. The advantage of our novel therapeutic over existing drugs is that it can also be used to visualize primary and metastatic lesions in vivo by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Studies in cats with mammary carcinoma will help bring this therapeutic into clinic to treat human breast cancer.

records.title: Observational Study of a Novel Canine Cancer Diet
records.current_registry_description:
When patients undergo fractionated radiation therapy, maintaining appetite, consistent stools, and body weight are incredibly important for patient well-being and quality of life. The most common non-radiation complications in dogs undergoing these longer radiation protocols include diarrhea, vomiting or regurgitation, and decreased appetite. When these complications happen in patients, both owners and clinicians attempt to offer a multitude of foods, home cooked diets, probiotics, appetite stimulants, anti-nausea medications, or antibiotics. Recently nutritionists and veterinarians at a well-known pet food manufacturer developed a prescription diet designed to specifically help nourish and support dogs that are fighting cancer. This diet is highly digestible and contains a proprietary blend of prebiotic fibers to help support a healthy gastrointestinal microbiome to provide consistent stool quality. The goal of this study is to evaluate the acceptance of the novel diet through food intake and eating enthusiasm data by dogs undergoing daily, definitive intent radiation therapy, and to examine the differences in body weight changes, muscle condition scoring, body condition scoring, body fat index, quality of life, and stool consistency over time in dogs receiving the novel vs control diet.


If your dog participates in this study, he/she will have blood work, urine panel, fecal analysis, and will be randomized to receive one of the two study foods during radiation therapy. Blood work and fecal analysis will be performed prior to starting radiation therapy, half way through radiation, at the end of the radiation protocol and two weeks after completing radiation. Urine panel will be performed prior to starting radiation, at the final radiation dose, and at the two week recheck. We will assess intake of the diet and enthusiasm of the diet twice weekly. We ask that you also record food intake and eating enthusiasm twice a week, fecal scores at each defecation, and quality of life weekly with provided guides and questionnaires. You and your clinical team will be blinded to which diet your dog is receiving, but this will be revealed at the conclusion of the study period.

records.title: CAR T Cell and Verdinexor Therapy for Treatment of Glioma Tumors in Dogs
records.current_registry_description:
About the study


Every year, about 3 out of every 100 dogs will be diagnosed with a brain tumor. Many of these dogs will be diagnosed with a glioma tumor, which is the second most common type of brain tumor and also, unfortunately, the most difficult to treat. One of the most promising developing areas of research for treating glioma tumors is immunotherapy, which is a type of intervention that uses the dog's own cells to fight the cancer cells.


This study is looking at a specific type of immunotherapy called CAR T cell therapy. CAR T cells are created by doing a simple blood draw from the dog to extract the T cells ("fighter" cells), which are then infused with a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) protein. This "upgrade" allows the T cells to target and attack the glioma tumor cells. This intervention has been used in children with brain tumors but this study will be the first time it's being used in dogs with glioma tumors!


In addition to the immunotherapy, we will be looking at a specific type of chemotherapy that has shown extremely promising results in canine lymphoma, along with human glioma tumors. This chemotherapy drug, verdinexor, will be used in combination with the CAR T cell therapy in an effort to produce the best possible outcome.


Who qualifies


Dogs who are over 10kg (22lb) in body weight who have already had a brain tumor diagnosed on MRI.

Tumor must be surgically accessible to allow for biopsy and injection of CAR T cells directly into the tumor

Dogs must be healthy enough to safely undergo anesthesia for the biopsy of the tumor

Dogs cannot have previously received chemotherapy or radiation for this tumor


Study activities and Timeline


Visit 1 | Day-17

  1. Exam
  2. Blood draw to create CAR T cells
  3. Begin verdinexor (chemo) therapy twice per week

Visit 2 | Days -4 and -3

  1. On both days, we will give a drug that temporarily depletes the immune system to prepare your dog's body for the CAR T cell injection

Visit 3 | Days 0, 1, and 3

  1. The first day will consist of the first CAR T cell injection while the next 2 days consist of recheck exams

Visit 4 | Days 8 - 10

  1. The visits throughout these days will consist of a brief planning scan followed by the brain biopsy surgery. During the surgery, a second injection of CAR T cells will be given directly into the tumor.

Visit 5 | Month 3

  1. We will do a recheck a MRI to evaluate the tumor response


Verdinexor will continue to be given at home twice weekly until the tumor progresses based on neurological signs or growth seen on MRI.

records.title: Electrochemotherapy for Nasal Cancer
records.current_registry_description:
Nasal Cancers in dogs and cats are uncommon and standard treatment is external beam radiation therapy. Side effects from radiation therapy may sometimes be severe and not every patient will qualify or respond to this therapy. Plus, there are significant delays in accommodating patients for timely radiation therapy treatment due to the paucity of centers and available specialists.


Nasal Electrochemotherapy has been used predominantly outside of the United States (see below).


Radiol Oncol 2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430.

 doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec.

Minimally Invasive Electrochemotherapy Procedure for Treating Nasal Duct Tumors in Dogs using a Single Needle Electrode

Felipe Maglietti 1 2 3, Matías Tellado 4, Nahuel Olaiz 1 2 3, Sebastian Michinski 1 2 3, Guillermo Marshall 1 2 3


Abstract

Background: Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we use electrochemotherapy (ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors.

Materials and methods: In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.

Results: In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treated nasal passage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively.

Conclusions: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treat nasal tumors with encouraging results.


We now have a nasal electrochemotherapy electrode here in the United States.


Clinical Protocol involves selected patients to receive a short sedation with IV propofol, +/- dexdomitor and O2 via intubation. Bleomycin IV 8 minutes prior to electrode placement into both nares providing a short pulse which opens the cell membranes driving chemotherapy to the region being treated. In this case, we begin treatment at the deepest point of the nasal cavity just proximal to the region of the cribiform plate (end of nasal cavity). After each treatment, the electrode is moved proximally until the entire region of both nasal cavities are treated. Side effects are minimal and patients will go home on 3 days of anti-inflammatory medication. This is an out-patient procedure.

The overall goal is to use this new research medication that is specific to prostate cancer cells to kill the cancer.

records.title: Nanoparticle CRT Combined with High Frequency Ultrasound with or without Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Dogs with Advanced Melanoma
records.current_registry_description: This is a randomized two-arm pilot study comparing dogs with advanced melanoma treated with nanoparticle calreticulin based immunotherapy combined with a focused ultrasound (HIFU) with or without an immune checkpoint inhibitor (anti-PDL-1). We have previously demonstrated that delivering a calreticulin (CRT) expression plasmid via a cationic liposome nanoparticle (CRT-NP) generates an immunostimulatory signal in mice tumors, akin to the immunogenic cell death-associated external cell membrane-bound CRT induced by radiation. CRT is a well-known multifunctional chaperone protein involved in cellular calcium homeostasis and immune modulation. The primary aim of this study is to evaluate local and systemic (abscopal) immune effects of CRT-NP based immunotherapy in combination with HIFU with and without an anti-PDL-1 monoclonal antibody (immune checkpoint inhibitor). Dogs will receive CRT-NP intratumorally once weekly for 4-8 weeks along with HIFU applied weekly to the same tumors. An anti-PDL-1 monoclonal antibody will be administered intravenously every 2 weeks, three days post HIFU treatment. Dogs will undergo baseline comprehensive lab work and urinalysis, which will also be monitored throughout treatment. A baseline CT scan or radiographs will be performed and repeated 12 weeks after the start of treatment to monitor for metastasis/progression of disease. Tumor volume will be measured at each visit along with adverse event reporting at each visit as well according to the VCOG Criteria for Adverse Events v. 2020. Tumor biopsies will be performed to monitor immune modulation, T cell infiltration, myeloid markers, and cytokine response. Dogs with a durable response will be monitored long term every 2-3 months. This study has been approved by the UTSW Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

records.title: Treating Dogs With Glioma Using Radiation and Immunotherapy
records.current_registry_description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that pose significant therapeutic challenges in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by locally invasive growth and poor overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds—particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers—are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy may also be used as a standalone treatment, delivered through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT). SRT offers the advantages of high precision, greater tissue sparing, and shorter treatment duration. Despite these interventions, the prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. Their natural disease course, intact immune system, and clinically comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable for evaluating the efficacy and safety of emerging therapies.

One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy. In this study, we investigate the combination of stereotactic radiation therapy with an FDA-approved nanoparticle, previously shown to be safe in dogs. This nanoparticle has demonstrated the ability in rodent models to modulate the tumor immune microenvironment by transforming tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from an M2 (pro-tumor) to an M1 (anti-tumor) phenotype.

records.current_registry_description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that present a significant therapeutic challenge in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by their locally invasive behavior and limited overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds, particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers, are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Radiotherapy can be delivered alone also, through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT), the latter offering greater precision and tissue sparing and short duration treatments. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. The natural disease progression, intact immune system, and comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable in assessing therapeutic efficacy and safety.

A pivotal safety study of CAR neutrophils in dogs was recently conducted at Purdue University, followed by preclinical efficacy testing in murine models of glioma. These genetically modified cells showed potential in targeting brain tumors with minimal off-target toxicity. Building upon these encouraging results, our current research proposes to evaluate the combined therapeutic effect of CAR immunotherapy and radiation therapy in dogs diagnosed with glioma. The rationale is to transform the tumor microenvironment through CAR neutrophils, potentially enhancing the efficacy and outcome of radiation therapy. This synergistic approach may not only improve survival in canine patients but also provide critical translational insights for the treatment of glioblastoma in humans.

records.title: Characterization of Soft Tissue Sarcoma Microscopic Extension
records.current_registry_description:
The goal of the study is to assess the microscopic extension of soft tissue sarcomas. records.title: Finding draining lymph nodes for anal gland tumors in dogs using minimally invasive surgery
records.current_registry_description: Anal sac cancers in dogs often spread to other areas of the body. This is called metastasis. Local lymph nodes are a common site for the cancer to spread in dogs with anal sac tumors. Removing lymph nodes with cancer improves outcome. However, assessment of the lymph nodes that drain fluid from a tumor can be challenging. A safe and common test is sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping. This is where we test the first lymph node(s) that drain fluid from a tumor for cancer cells. It has been used in dogs with anal sac cancer. However, the lymph nodes that drain anal sac tumors are located within the abdomen and pelvis. So far SLN mapping on dogs with anal sac tumors has needed open abdominal surgery. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. This is where small incisions are made for cameras and instruments, and tissue can be removed without making a large incision. We have successfully done SLN mapping for anal sac cancer with MIS techniques in dog cadavers. We want to evaluate these SLN mapping techniques via a MIS approach in dogs with anal sac tumors. We also want to see how this compares to a previously studied method called CT-lymphography that is done before surgery. Our goal is to obtain important cancer care information from SLN mapping, but with the potential benefits of MIS compared to open abdominal surgery.

records.title: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
records.current_registry_description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in dogs, specially in large size breeds and it presents a high biological aggressiveness, in many cases at the time of diagnosis, metastatic dissemination has already occurred. However, despite initial therapeutic response, patients develop treatment resistance, leading to the presence of metastasis, most commonly within the lungs, reducing life expectancy and quality of life of the patient. 

Recently the use of liquid biopsies, a minimally invasive sample collection from body fluids, such as blood, has been increasing, as they detect specific molecular biomarkers. Liquid biopsies can aid in the detection of certain pathologies, monitor disease progression or recurrence after the treatment, the latter can be achieved by measuring molecules such as proteins and microRNAs that are in the circulating blood. These proteins and microRNA might provide less invasive and faster detection than other techniques, such as computerized tomography (CT scan).

To achieve the previous, we are looking for canine patients, over 25 kg (55.11 lbs) that have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma, and have not undergone amputation of the affected limb.

records.title: Nasal Cancer Treatment with Electrochemotherapy
records.current_registry_description:
Nasal cancer in dogs and cats are uncommon with carcinomas being most common in dogs. Treatment has been limited to external beam radiation therapy at significant expense and often multiple days of anesthesia needed. Median survival is about 1 year and side effects are common. Electrochemotherapy is the use of electrical impulses to open cell membranes driving chemotherapy locally, i.e. a targeted therapy.


We now have an electrode that may be used for nasal tumors based on published material below:.


Radiol Oncol.2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430. doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec. Minimally InvasiveElectrochemotherapyProcedure for TreatingNasalDuct Tumors inDogs using a Single Needle Electrode. Maglietti F,Tellado M,Olaiz N,Michinski S,Marshall G


Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we useelectrochemotherapy(ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors. MATERIALS AND METHODS:In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.RESULTS:In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treatednasalpassage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treatnasaltumors with encouraging results. Those clients not electing to participate with this therapy will be followed and data used for comparison. Rechecks may also be done with RDVM but advanced imaging post treatment would be necessary to follow response. While the study is for canine patients, there is no reason not to look at feline and wildlife with the same or similar diagnosis.


The procedure involves a short general anesthesia and is generally an outpatient procedure. Minimal side-effects have been noted and anti-inflammatory pain management may be necessary for a few days post procedure

records.title: CHOP vs. LOPP chemotherapy as a first line treatment for naïve peripheral T cell lymphoma in dogs
records.current_registry_description: Lymphoma comprises approximately 25% of all canine cancers. Up to 40% of these cases are caused by T lymphocytes, known as peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL). The vast majority of lymphoma cases cannot be addressed with surgery and instead warrant chemotherapy. The standard of care chemotherapy protocol for lymphoma is abbreviated CHOP, which stands for the 4 drugs involved. Generally, dogs with PTCL treated with CHOP chemotherapy tend to experience shorter remission durations and overall survival than dogs with diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). When treated with CHOP chemotherapy, PTCL dogs have a median survival time of 4-9 months while DLBCL dogs have a median survival time of 11-13 months. Previous studies have questioned whether other, non-CHOP protocols may be better suited for dogs with PTCL in hopes of increasing remission and survival times. One protocol that has been repeatedly investigated is LOPP chemotherapy. This protocol uses two of the same drugs as CHOP and two that are different. Recent studies have demonstrated with dogs with PTCL treated with LOPP can experience survival times closer to 11-17 months. While these findings are promising, none of these investigations have had a control arm of dogs receiving CHOP chemotherapy. The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL. In this study, your dog will be randomly selected to receive either CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. At each visit, their lymph node size, blood work, and overall wellbeing will be assessed. Both protocols involve treatments every 7-14 days and take 4-6 months to complete. Following protocol completion, your pet will return once monthly to assess remission status.

The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the safety and anti-cancer activity of fibroblast activation protein (FAP) targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, alone or in combination with orally administered immunotherapy drugs, in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. FAP is a protein that is expressed on the surface of tumor cell and can be recognized by a T cell. CAR T cells are when a patient’s own cancer fighting white blood cells are modified to express a receptor which binds a specific molecule expressed on the surface of a tumor cell. The two oral immunotherapy drugs being used in combination with FAP CAR T cells (losartan and toceranib [Palladia]) have already been extensively evaluated in a prior trial in dogs with bone cancer and have demonstrated considerable anti-cancer activity, with minimal toxicity. Studies in rodent models of cancer and in vitro in human and canine OS cell lines have indicated that FAP CAR T cells can exert robust killing of canine OS cells and may complement the activities of toceranib and losartan. Therefore, this trial is designed to determine whether FAP CAR T cells are safe alone and in combination with losartan and toceranib, and if losartan and toceranib can improve tumor infiltration of FAP CAR T cells.


At the start of the study, dogs will have blood drawn (~3 ½ tablespoons) to be used for generation of the CAR T cells. Dogs will also be sedated to have a small sample of their tumor taken for study purposes. They will return 10 days later for an exam, bloodwork, and for oral chemotherapy to reduce the number of normal lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell) to maximize the effectiveness of the CAR T cells. A second dose of chemotherapy will be given at home by the owner the following day. Dogs will then return 14 days after the initial visit for an exam, blood and urine tests, blood collection for study purposes, and CAR T cell infusion. The infusion is given over 15 minutes, and then dogs will stay in the hospital until the end of the day for monitoring. Dogs will return 3 and 7 days later for an exam, blood and urine tests, and blood collection for study purposes. Fourteen days after the CAR T infusion, the tumor will be removed surgically. Visits will be required 2 and 6 weeks after surgery for an exam, blood/urine tests, and blood collection for the study. The study is complete after the visit 6 weeks post-surgery (total study duration of 10 weeks).

Abstract

Immunotherapy has changed the treatment landscape for cancer over the past decade. records.title: Immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
records.current_registry_description:
Oral melanoma is a highly aggressive disease with poor outcomes and no effective treatments. Our recent research has shown that a weakened form of the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is safe, and can trigger strong anti-tumor effects.


By injecting a small amount of this weakened virus directly into the tumor, we aim to activate the dog's immune system to fight the cancer. Additionally, we will collect and expand immune cells from the tumor, as these cells are more likely to recognize and attack cancer cells. These enhanced immune cells will then be reinfused into the patient to target existing or potential metastatic disease.


To evaluate our therapy, we will first perform a tumor biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and analyze the immune cells already present (Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes). We will then inject the tumor with the weakened virus. One week later, the tumor will be surgically removed, and immune cells from the cancer will be expanded for future use if metastases are present or develop later. After treatment, we will closely monitor the patients through periodic blood tests and imaging (CT scans) every three months.


A small group of dogs (randomly selected) will be the control, and while not receiving the virus injection, they will have their immune cells extracted from the tumor and expanded to be reinfused in case of progressive disease.


Cost of tumor biopsy, two CT imaging sessions, trial-related blood work, the viral reagent and injections, the collection priming and reinjection of the immune cells. Additionally, participating dogs are eligible to receive a $800 post-trial incentive.

records.current_registry_description:
Myc (a family of transcription factors encompassing c-, N-, and L-Myc) is a pleiotropic, evolutionarily conserved transcription factor. records.title: Combinatorial Imaging with PDL1-IRDye800 to Guide Surgical Treatment of Oral Cancer
records.current_registry_description:
Background and purpose


For dogs diagnosed with oral cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma), curative intent surgical removal has been consistently found to have the longest remission rate. However, conventional diagnostic imaging, which we use to plan our surgery, is imperfect and can underestimate the extent of the tumor which results in the potential that not all cancer cells are removed during surgery. This directly impacts patient outcomes (disease free interval and overall survival). There is a critical need to improve our ability to detect cancer intraoperatively (i.e. during the surgery) to improve patient outcomes.


Further, for human head and neck cancer the standard of care is to give immunotherapy (drugs that improve the immune system's ability to fight off cancer) prior to surgery, which has resulted in increased survival in a subset of patients. We have no data on this type of pre-surgical treatment in dogs, and if it would also improve patient survival times.


The purpose of this study is to evaluate the use of a theranostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) before surgery to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer. This agent is an immunotherapeutic drug (anti-PDL1) bound to a fluorophore. This drug would be given 2X before treatment (surgery or other).


Through this study we will determine if this drug can allow us to see residual cancer cells during surgery (differentiate cancer from healthy tissue) and if treatment of the tumor before surgery with the drug can improve the local anti-tumor immune response (decrease in percent viable cells in the tumor).


If successful this could overall vastly improve our ability to treat oral cancer in dogs.


What happens in this study


  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical examination, full blood work, urinalysis
  2. A pre-operative biopsy performed at enrollment, to confirm squamous cell carcinoma or melanoma
  3. Intravenous administration of the anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 theranostic probe twice before surgery
  4. Near infrared fluorescence Imaging performed at 8 hours, 24 hours, and 48 hours after probe delivery
  5. Repeat biopsy or curative intent surgery after the second anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 probe administration
  6. Follow-up visits at 7 days and 4 weeks

records.title: Pilot Study for a New Quasiorganelle Therapy in Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
records.current_registry_description:
Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive cancer in dogs that often does not respond well to standard treatments like chemotherapy or radiation. While some dogs experience benefits, these treatments affect many cells at once and cannot adapt as a tumor changes. New research shows that cancer closely interacts with the immune system and surrounding tissues, suggesting that better treatments may need to work inside cells, not just target them from the outside. Quasiorganelle therapy is an experimental approach that aims to do this by using weakened, non-disease-causing bacteria derived from Listeria monocytogenes to deliver helpful genetic instructions directly into immune and tumor cells, with the goal of improving how the body recognizes and responds to cancer.


The first group (8 dogs) will receive quasiorganelle therapy alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the quasiorganelle infusion. They will then be observed for up 4 days at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center and blood and fecal samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return for treatment once weekly for 4 doses followed by 2 weeks off. This schedule will then be repeated two more times for a total of 16 weeks of treatment. Imaging to determine alterations in tumor size will be repeated at the end of each 4 week treatment period.

The second group (8 dogs) will receive quaisorganelle therapy that includes gene therapy. Their treatment and monitoring schedule will be identical to that of the first group.

Following the 16 week treatment period, dogs will return for evaluation every 4 weeks or until progressive disease is documented.


Please note: While enrolled, dogs should not live with anyone who is pregnant or planning to become pregnant.

records.title: Combination of electrochemotherapy and gene therapy with canine IL-12
records.current_registry_description:
Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is an advanced treatment in veterinary oncology. It has been routinely used in dogs for treating mast cell tumors, carcinomas and soft tissue sarcomas, in cats for SCC, carcinomas and sarcomas and in horses for sarcoid tumors. ECT is a local ablative technique which has a good local anti-tumor control in dogs (up to 70%) and in cats (up to 80%) and in horses up to 100% but limited impact on distant tumors and metastasis. Therefore, there is a need for a combination therapy which could provide local control with a systemic effect to battle cancer spread. Interleukin 12 is a potent immune stimulator that works by increasing IFN gamma which has an anti-tumor effects through the activation of cytotoxic cells such as natural killer cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. IL-12 also up-regulates antigen presenting cells making the tumor cells recognizable to the immune system. Several clinical studies have already been performed treating different canine tumors by electro-genetransfer with a plasmid encoding IL-12. Results showed increased systemic IL-12 and IFN gamma with an effect on distant metastasis .

The treatment will be performed in patients under a short general anesthesia. Depending on the tumor volume and the response the treatments will be repeated every 3-4 weeks. Responses will be followed with physical exam and imaging (X-rays or CT). Electrochemotherapy will be performed using direct intra-tumoral application of IL-12 (2mg per patient) and the intravenous application of bleomycin (standard dose). The study is based on multiple publications showing benefit with this combination with control of the cancer including metastasis and minimal to no adverse effects to the patients.

records.title: Exploring a Nonoparticle-enabled Treatment of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Cats
records.current_registry_description:
For veterinary patients, surgery is the primary treatment for many tumour types. Surgery may not always be the best option for cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) as it is challenging to obtain adequate clear surgical margins and often, the disease reoccurs. Adjuvant therapies including chemotherapy, radiation therapy and palliative options are ineffective or poorly tolerated and do not improve the overall survival rate of cats with OCSCC. We need to make improvements to staging and treatment.

PORPHYSOMES (pPs) are a novel nanomedicine developed and supplied by Professor Dr Gang Zheng’s Laboratory (University Health Network, Toronto). These particles are delivered intravenously (in a local vein through a catheter) and concentrate in areas with tumour cells (either the primary tumour location or where the cancer has spread (metastatic site). pPs can be used to highlight the tumour by using a specialized technique called near-infrared fluorescence imaging (NIRF). This equipment allows for image-guided surgery, tumour margin assessment and lymph node staging. pPs can also be used to in combination with photoablation – photodynamic therapy (PDT) to deliver treatment directly to the tumour. 

 

pPs-enabled therapies can have an immediate impact on cancer management providing better patient outcomes. This study offers a novel approach to the treatment of OCSCC in cats. The use of pPs is ground-breaking translational research and the information gained will be used to treat future dogs, cats and humans with cancer. A human clinical trial is planned to be conducted in 2024.

records.title: Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
records.current_registry_description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs and, while amputation followed by systemic chemotherapy is the standard of care, it may not be the most appropriate treatment option for all dogs or it may not meet the goals of individual owners. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been utilized to kill tumor cells while leaving the affected limb intact showing good primary tumor control rates. The biggest risk with using SBRT in this setting is the potential for pathologic fracture of the affected limb. Here we plan to use a dual energy CT for radiation planning and to quantify bone mineral density (BMD) both before and after SBRT to assess changes that happen with SBRT treatment. BMD measures calcium and other minerals. In theory, the more mineral, the denser and stronger the bone is and less likely it is to break. In addition, we will measure bone breakdown markers before and after treatment to determine how these are correlated with the BMD and response to treatment.


Once enrolled, dogs will have blood and urine collected for bone breakdown markers followed by 3 doses (or fractions) of SBRT. On the third and final fraction, dogs will receive the first dose of standard of care chemotherapy (carboplatin). Two weeks after chemotherapy, your dog will need to have a complete blood count performed to assess response to chemotherapy as well as blood and urine collected for the bone breakdown markers. At each dose of chemotherapy, a total of 6, blood and urine will be collected to assess trends in these markers. At the time of the final chemotherapy treatment, an additional dual energy CT will be performed to assess the changes that happen to the bone after treatment. Once chemotherapy is complete, it is recommended that your dog return every 8 weeks for chest x-rays; blood and urine will be collected for the study at the 1st 3 visits post-chemotherapy. At any change in lameness or concern for progression of disease, it is expected that your dog will return to CSU for assessment and evaluation of the bone markers.

records.title: Dose escalation study for a novel STING agonist in tumor-bearing dogs
records.current_registry_description:
Immunotherapy, engaging the power of the immune system against cancer, has become a standard part of oncology care. One such approach utilizes the STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) pathway. Our colleagues at University of Michigan, led by Dr. James Moon, have developed a drug that activates the STING pathway. This drug, called CMP-002, has been shown to combat cancer in a laboratory setting, with and without the use of another modulator of immune system, PD-1 blockade. This success prompted a collaboration with Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine as we hope to contribute to efforts that can help veterinary oncology patients and humans alike. Our initial studies, led by Dr. Vilma Yuzbasiyan-Gurkan at MSU, established the dose range tolerated in healthy dogs.

The purpose of this study is to confirm the best dose of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade for tumor-bearing dogs. CMP-002 has already been tested in healthy dogs. It is not uncommon for patients with cancer to process drugs differently, which is why we intend to confirm the best dose for tumor-bearing dogs. The findings of this study will then be used in future studies assessing the anti-cancer properties of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade.


There will be two study groups:


The first group of patients (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will visit their primary veterinarians one week later for blood sampling. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second infusion. records.title: Mammary tumors in cats
records.current_registry_description:
Surgery is the most common treatment used for mammary cancer in cats. The pathologist determines whether surgery has removed all cancer cells many days after the procedure. We need rapid and accurate testing during surgery to detect residual cancer to decrease cancer recurrence and the necessity for repeated surgery or treatments.


Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. We have performed some initial evaluations using this optical coherence tomography for detection of residual cancer, which has had very encouraging results.


Cats will undergo surgery to remove their tumor; following removal, the tumor will be scanned with polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to assess the surgical margins for residual cancer cells. The specimen will then undergo thorough histopathological assessment.


The overall purpose of the study is to evaluate a new imaging method to detect cancer cells left behind following removal of mammary tumors in client-owned cats undergoing surgery. This technology has been used successfully in human breast cancer surgery, providing microscopic assessment of surgical margins within minutes. Identifying a rapid and thorough imaging method to detect any remaining cancer cells during surgery for mammary tumors will support targeted treatment management decisions and improve outcomes for cats and dogs with cancer.


Pet owners are financially responsible for all costs associated with evaluation and surgery. Each pet owner receiving surgery at OSU will receive a $70 credit to their account to cover the costs of the histopathology evaluation.

records.title: Electrochemotherapy for Bone Cancer
records.current_registry_description:
Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).


Curr Oncol. 2022 Mar 4;29(3):1672-1682. doi: 10.3390/curroncol29030139.

Electrochemotherapy Is Effective in the Treatment of Bone Metastases

Laura Campanacci 1, Luca Cevolani 1, Francesca De Terlizzi 2, Laura Saenz 3, Nikolin Alì 1, Giuseppe Bianchi 1, Davide Maria Donati 1


Abstract

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the use of ECT in patients with metastatic bone disease, demonstrating that it does not damage the mineral structure of the bone and its regenerative capacity, and that is feasible and efficient for the treatment of bone metastases. Since 2009, 88 patients with bone metastasis have received ECT at the Rizzoli Institute. 2014 saw the start of a registry of patients with bone metastases treated with ECT, whose data are recorded in a shared database. We share the Rizzoli Institute experience of 38 patients treated with ECT for a bone metastasis, excluding patients not included in the registry (before 2014) and those treated with bone fixation. Mean follow-up was 2 months (1-52). Response to treatment using RECIST criteria was 29% objective responses, 59% stable disease, and 16% progressive disease. Using PERCIST, the response was 36% OR, 14% SD, and 50% PD with no significant differences between the two criteria. A significant decrease in pain and better quality of life was observed at follow up.


Clinical protocol: Patient will be anesthetized and the lytic area of bone to be treated identified. Using a Jamshidi bone needle, a core will be created allowing placement of the linear bone electrode into the lesion. Once in place, targeted electrochemotherapy will be applied into the lytic lesion. Bleomycin will be injected IV and after 8 minutes the pulse will be sent into the bone lesion allowing a transient opening of the cell membrane. 2- 3 treatments will be completed and the area wrapped upon recovery.


Follow up imaging in 4 and 8 weeks with radiographs.

records.title: Clinical trial for dogs newly diagnosed with osteosarcoma
records.current_registry_description:
In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of immune cells known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells, made from the blood of a healthy donor dog, in dogs with bone cancer. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that have been shown to kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. The iNKT cells directly kill the tumor (cancer cell) and  they also boost the patient's own anti-tumor (cancer-killing) immune responses. In this study, we will genetically modify these natural killer T cells (NKT) cells to express a protein known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the genetically modified CAR-iNKT cells to a target protein (known as B7H3) on the bone cancer cell. The CAR-iNKT cells kill the bone cancer cells and activate the immune system to do the same. The purpose of this study is to determine i) the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, ii) their ability to traffic to the bone tumor in your dog’s leg and exert an anti-cancer effect there, iii) their ability to delay or prevent metastatic disease and iv) how long the CAR-iNKT cells remain in your dog’s body. 


This clinical trial is fully funded and at no cost to owners. Covered procedures include:

  1. Bloodwork for general health screening
  2. Chest radiographs to be sure the osteosarcoma has not spread to the lungs prior to treatment
  3. Bone biopsy to confirm osteosarcoma and the presence of the B7H3 target protein
  4. Cellular therapy with iNKT cells
  5. Amputation of the affected limb (~10 days after cell therapy) and all post-op care/hospitalization
  6. Standard of care chemotherapy
  7. Follow up monitoring of bloodwork and chest radiographs


All clinical trial visits are in person at the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

records.title: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients
records.current_registry_description:
WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). 


The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe.


The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects.  


The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient.

records.title: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor
records.current_registry_description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.


Dogs enrolled in this study will receive a single dose of radiation therapy, followed by recheck visits 7 days and 28 days after treatment. At each of these visits, patients will have tumor measurements and small samples of their masses collected with a needle for analysis. Patients complete the study on day 28 or if their tumor progresses after radiation treatment. At that time, patients with persistent tumors are eligible to receive $1000 towards the cost of standard chemotherapy treatment.

records.title: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
records.current_registry_description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats.


Cats will receive four injections of the LTN immunotherapy into their tumor, which are given once every three weeks. Cats must be put under anesthesia for these injections. While under anesthesia, cats will have CT scans and tumor biopsies performed prior to starting treatment, at the time of the third injection, and 3 weeks after the 4th injection (CT only). Blood tests (complete blood count and chemistry profile) will also be performed at these visits. Study participation is completed after the visit that is 3 weeks after the last injection. A total of 5 visits and anesthetic episodes are required for this study.

records.title: PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma
records.current_registry_description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.

Study number: VCCT-26-014
